A war correspondent describes a
maternity hospital and children's
home in North Germany, we'll
equipped and fully stated, evidently
maintained for the offspring of
high-ranking and influential Nazis
who chose their mates for the pur-
pose of reproducing future leaders
of the master race. Some fifty or
more youngsters were there, living
under the best conditions and care,
and the reporter says that what to
do with them represents problem
for the military officials of the
Bremen port command. The par
ents apparently were designated by
code numbers, the key to which has
not been found.


Near Weimar, in Central Ger
many, in the concentration camp
at Buchenwald. liberating Amer
leans found another group of chill
dren. There were about a thou
sand boys there, under fourteen
years old, fatherless and mother
less. Their parents had been ex-
terminated as unacceptable to the
master race, or had died from suf-
fering and disease. They had been
brought there from all over Europe
and when the Americans found
these boys and segregated them
from other prisoners for special
treatment, most of them were mere
wraith-like specters of childhood.
Nobody knows what will become of
them, either.


But as the full details of Nazi
degradation are supplied, what to
do with those responsible for it be-
comes less and less of problem.
Their guilt cries out for punish
ment that will symbolic the indig
nation of a shocked world.

| ABOARD A BATTLESHIP OFF
TWO JIMA. Jan. "a Via Navy
Radio (Delayed) Striking 75O
miles from Tokyo, this mighty
battleship, accompanied by cruis-
ers and destroyers, pounded Two
Jima today, seeking to blast the
Ienemy's underground positions
on this last major stronghold
southeast of Japan.


(This is the first disclosure that


battleship participated in bonn


harding the fortresslike island)


Cruising slowly along the shore,
the task group ripped the island
from the level lands on the north to
the dominating peak on the south
ern tip.


Only when storm clouds and rain
forced the withdrawal of spotting
planes did the relentless lombard
ment of the 16-inch rifles of the
battleship, the 8-inchers OF the
cruisers and the smaller guns of the
destroyers halt.


AS the force steamed away, three
cargo ships were left in wreckage.
One probably loaded with gasoline
exploded, the giant blast hurting
fame and smoke high above the
550-foot volcanic peak. The two
others were beached, burning
fiercely.


Ships Burn.


Occasional explosions sped the
flames of the burning ships.


On the little island, by 2 miles,
which dominates the Volcano group,
hundreds of shells tore into the
airf1elds, heavy artillery positions,
unloading and dock areas and dual
purpose batteries.


L was very well satisfied with the
results. All primary targets were
pin-pointed," said the commander
of the force.


II believe the approach was vir-
tuallNa surprise to the enemy until
just preceding the bombardment, E"
the task force commander con-
tinued.


Earlier in the day the island had
been pounded by bombs, with B-29s
participating in the co-ordinated
strike which took the task force
deep into Japans home waters.
Opposition Is Lacking.


Throughout the assault the Japa-
nese failed to give any material op-
position.


Eight enemy planes were seen and
five were destroyed. They made only
half-hearted attempts to attack.
One sped from the island field to-
ward the battleship, but was forced
to turn off and shot down in flames
by the destroyers' guns. Another
crashed in the sea, two were de-
stroyed on the ground and a fifth
was probably shot down by spot
ting plane.


Enemy coastal batteries were
turned on the destroyers which
darted close inshore, but were si-
lenced in short order to end the
meager opposition to the hour-and-
a-half bombardment under brilliant
sunlight. Todayb attack was the
second of the year and the sixth of
the war.

HARRISONBURG, Va, April 23.-
State troopers and local officers are
searching for motorists believed re-
sponsible for seven fires which
burned more than $50 acres in the
George Washington National Forest
Saturday and yesterday.


The fires, brought under control
yesterday by more than 200 fire.
fighters, originated along U. S.
Route $50 across Shenandoah Noun
tain in Augusta and Highland
Counties.


The location of the fires indicated
they were of incendiary origin, M.
c. Howard, forest supervisor, said,
adding that he believed that per-
sons travelling along the highway
in an automobile started the fires.


The forest was dry and the wind
was high, causing forest rangers
to call for help from fire wardens in
Rockingham, Highland,
Bath and Allegheny Counties before
the flames could be checked.

BADKISSINGEN, Germany, July

stedt disliked the idea of q sep
arate German air force because of
the troubles encountered getting
tactical support from the Luftwaffe
and would have preferred the liai-
son system used by Allied air and
ground leaders.


The German commander in the
west expressed these views in an
interview this month with Mai.
Gen. Oliver P. Weyland, commander
Of the 9th Air Force and former
commander of the 18th Tactical
Air Command which battered Won
Rundstedt'S armies with fighter
bombers and medium bonlbers.


Gen. Weyland asked the question
to obtain the enemy'S views on the
value of our tactics and to attempt
to learn how and why the Nazi
air force failed.


British Doubt Story.


1--WE unfortunately did not have
close coordination" Won Rundstedt
said. I'VE had to go to the Luft-
waite and plead with them"


A high British officer, questioned
about that later, said it was just
the excuse of beaten general and
the fact was that the Germans
never really understood air war and
never had either enough or the
proper types of warplaneS.


Won Rundstedt said the Luft-
waite co-operated 100 per cent in
the Polish campaign and provided
satisfactory support during the at
tack on France. Then it deterior-
ated, he said, pointing out that the
Luftwaffe declined in relative
strength compared with Allied air.
forces. He also noted that the Nazis
never sent up more than 400 fight
erS in one day.


In this respect the British official
said he felt the Luftwaffe was
beaten before the Sicily landing,
whereas American officials date its
demise in May of 1914.


Won Runstedt said that because
Of "Goering's anxiety to keep the
air force an independent branch of
the service" there was no inter
change of staff officers between the
air and ground forces.


Lack of Planes Cited.


He said also that when the Luft-
waite lacked aircraft for all its
trained personnel the surplus men
were not transferred to the regular
ground forces, as was done in the
United States Army, but were kept
in separate field divisions of the
air force, where the proper results
never were obtained.


Won Runstedt said he believed the
entire German air force should have
been operated from a central pool
rather than parceled out among the
various armies and corps.


Won Runstedt expressed the view
that the Americans should have
used more tactical air effort at night.
since the moral effect would have
more than offset any decreased &C
curacy." He said the V weapons
came six months too late.

today that Britain and France have

Signed in London to-day, the
British-French agreement provides
for close alignment of policy in the

tling unrest marked seven months

demand for independence from
France.


''The two governments" said an

nized that it was in their Joint in
terest to encourage, within the

ration, the economic well being and
security of the peoples of the Mid
die East"

Syria and Lebanon started last May
when Syrian demands for complete
independence from France devel-
oped into armed clashes. The
French shelled Damascus and more
than 400 were reported killed and
several hundred more wounded in
sporadic disturbances.


The Syrians charged the French
with reinforcing their troops in the
midst of negotiations.


British and Free French forces
marched into the country on June 8
1941, promising to grant independ-
ence. This independence subse-
quently was proclaimed by the
French, but Allied forces continued
to occupy the country because OF
war conditions and the mandate
legally still remained in existence.

President. Truman's chances Tor
gaining broad powers to reorganlze
the Government appeared much,
brighter today, following favorable
action on his request yesterday by
the House Committee on Expendl-I
lures in the executive department.


While they are expected to retain
the provisions of Chairman ManaS-
co.'s reorganization bill, which spe-
cifically exempted 81 Federal agen-
cies from any presidential revamp-
ing plan, the committee approved a
measure exempting only three units
of the Government from possible re-
organization.


The committee decided that the
Interstate Commerce Commission,
the Federal Trade Commission and
the Securities and Exchange Com
mission should be completely ex-
empted. This was done, members
said, because they are quasi judicial
and should be free from executive
domination. Another limitation
provides that the civil functions OF
the Engineer Corps of the War De-
partment may not be moved to any
other agency. These are such ac-
tivities as power projects and river
and harbor control, in which the
Army engineers participate with
various local government. The pow
ers would end July l, 1948.


Committee members said this date
was fixed for two reasons-first. it
is the end of a fiscal year; second,
it means any reorganization plan
cannot be placed before Congress
during presidential campaign
months and thus become a political
issue.


Mr.. Truman had asked for sweep
ing authority without any exemp-
tions. The committee first decided
on the half-a-loaf principle, but
changed its mind after Controller
General Lindsay Warren urged that
exemptions either be left out or
cut down to a minimum for real
economy"
Judiciary Committee has about
completed it's hearing on a similar
reorganization bill. Indications are
that the ICC, the SEC and several
other agencies will be exempted, as
in the bill approved by the House
committee.


Under terms of the bill, four other
agencies, the Civil Service Commis- |
sion. the Federal Communications
Commission, the Federal Power
Commission and the Veterans Ad-
ministration, cannot be reorganized
except under a separate plan for
each one

Perhaps you remember my telling
about the boy who asked for "a map
of what Germany will look like after
the war"


1, too, should like to have map
of that kind. but the new bound
aries will not be set until after a
peace treaty is drawn up and signed.


Yet these two points seem clear:


l. The country has been largely
wrecked


2. Germany will be smaller after
the peace treaty than it was in
1888


The wrecking of Germany started
long before the borders were crossed
by troops of the United Nations.
Hundreds of bombing raids had been
made. and scores of cities had been
struck.


! Hamburg. Berlin and Cologne
are among the German cities which
suffered fearful damage, both before
and after the crossing Of the bor-
derS.


The bombing plan for Germany
was laid out to destroy war factories,
gasoline centers and railway yards.
Yet bombardiers could hardly be ex-
pected to hit only those marks.
Countless houses have been shaken
down by blockbusters, townbusters
and other bombs.


The Nazi high command opened
the bombing of cities early in the
war. London and other British cities
suffered from German raids early in
the war. Then came the reply which
brought far more damage to Ger
many than had been done to Great
Britain.


War has come home to the Ger
man people Many of them NAV
say, quite truly, that they did not
approve of the war plans of Nazi
leaders, but the net result Is the
same. They have lost homes and
relatives amid their shattered cities.

A declaration that the Washing

part Of the District, instead of Vir-

Carran, Democrat. of Nevada, chair
man Of the Senate Judiciary Com
mittee.


Shortly after Chairman Randolph

yesterday reintroduced his bill of
last session to settle the century
old District-Virginia boundary dis
|pute, the Nevada Senator expressed
hope the issue would be settled, but
added the airport should not be
ceded to Virginia.


During the past Congress, Sena-
tor McCarran sponsored two bills
seeking to end confusion arising
from uncertainty Of the old hound
ary line, which has created a no
mans land" along the Virginia side
Of the Potomac.


One would have declared the air
port in the District, though other
wise fixing the boundary at the
present mean highwater mark on
the Virginia shore, as does the Ran
dolph bill. The latter bill, however
leaves the port within Virginia ter
ritory and, since it is federally
owned, reserves to the United States
concurrent jurisdiction over the air
port.


Senator McCarran, seeing little
chance Of action on his boundary
bill last session, also offered a bill
to apply District laws and regula-
tions to all the Federal reservations
In nearby Virginia without touch.
ing the boundary issue. That bill
also died with the old Congress,


Meanwhile, House District Com.
mittee spokesmen said the All
Transport Association, representins
81 operating air lines, had suggested
an amendment to the Randolph bill
which would treat the airport a.
an exclusive Federal jurisdiction

When Mrs. Martha Truman was
little girl Abraham Lincoln was
President. She has lived through an
age of wonders since then-the rail-
roads lacing the continent, the COM
ing of the telephone, the invention
OF the electric light, the debut of
the automobile, the development of
the radio, the birth of aviation and
any number of other marvels that
have revolutionized the life of
America and the world. Ninety-two
years old, she has seen so much
happen in her time that precious
little can surprise her now. Yet
even she, despite all her rich and
eventful years, must find it a truly
wonderful thing that today-after
her first trip by plane, on her first
visit to Washington-she is stopping
at the White House as the Nations
most distinguished mother. Pierce
was living there when she was born,
and after him Buchanan, and then
Lincoln, and then Johnson, and then
Grant, Hayes, Garfield, Arthur,
Cleveland, Mckinley, Theodore
Roosevelt, Taft, Wilson, Harding,
Coolidge, Hoover, Franklin Roosevelt,
and now her own son Harry. This
is an American story. Nothing quite
like it could take place anywhere
but in our country. All hail to this
remarkable, bright-eyed lady who
says "Fiddlesticks!" to people who
naturally make a fuss over her.

affairs.

GUAM, May 14.-Industrial
Nagoya, Japan's third largest

record feet of 500 American
Super Fortresses, and returning
crewmen reported sweeping
devastation" of the metropolis.


While there was no immediate re-
port of American losses, plane COM
manders agreed they must have been
very light, and said opposition was
surprisingly small.


Antiaircraft fire was described as
weak and inaccurate, and while

tion to fight.

Tokyo radio was reporting a con-
tinuing tWo-day offensive by 900
carrier based planes on its home is
lands. The carrier planes came
from two task forces. the uncon-
firmed enemy broadcast said.


The giant B-29 air parade was
more than 1900 miles long. The
first Super Fort had flown to the
Honshu Island city, dropped it's fire
bombs and had been on its way
home for 80 minutes when the last
plane was taking off from it's Mar
ianas base.


Results still were lacking here.


A new-type. six-pound fire bomb
was carried today for nearly every
one of Nagoya's 100000 inhabitants
Altogether. l,165,000 of the jelly
gasoline bombs were dropped. They
explode seconds after hitting the
target and spew flaming gasoline
over a sizable area.


Home Of Big Aircraft Works.


Nagoya, on Honshu, Is Japan's
largest aircraft industry center and
home of the Mitsubishi aircraft
engine works and others. One
quarter of the working population
lis engaged in warplane production.
The great aerial armada swept
over Two Jima for navigation
check-a fresh indication of the
value of that island.


The air feet later rendezvoused
off the japanese coast-defiant OF
interceptors-and the first bombar-
dier called bombs away" at 8:15
am.


Weather conditions were not the
best and the flyers were expected
to encounter cloud deck over the
target. However. bombing was
visual.


The general target area of to-
days raid was just west of the
gigantic Mitsubishi engine works
almost totally ruined in previous
attacks.


Five Areas Hammered.


Five great circles in the northern
section of the city, nine square miles
in all. were designated as target
areas. They included the Chigusa
factory of the Nagoya arsenal pro-
ducing heavy ordnance and am.
munition components; a large cleo.
trical plant, and thousands of home
factories turning out electrical parts
and airplane instruments.


Super Fortresses last attacked
Nagoya March 30 when a small
force hit the Mitsubishi plant
against light opposition. Five anc
four-tenths square miles of the city
had been burned out prior to today's
raid


Most Of Nagoya's construction Il

altitude today, attacking in 8

self was imprisoned at hard labor

STUART, Fla, Aug. 28.-Sheriff

store order.

Rioters Seize Camp.


The sheriff said the rioting la
horers took over the former Army

A call for help from the camp

trouble had not been determined.
AS soon as the cause and amount
of damage have been ascertained

Labor experts said, however, that
the probable cause was the laborers'
unWillingness to return to their
comparatively drab former exist
ence after sampling the high wages
and luxury goods during their en-
ployment in the United States.


State Police on Guard.


State highway pstrolmen were
standing by at the camp today on

and five deputies also were on hand

terday.


Sheriff Hancock said trouble had
been brewing for several days and
burst out yesterday with unexpected
fury.


The sheriff reported an enforced
quiet" at the camp today.


The outburst lasted three hours
and was touched off by the arrival
of 400 colored laborers who had
broken their contracts by misbe-
havior, Mr.. Hancock stated.


No Gunplay Reported.


With only War Food Administra-
ton employees on the scene to main
tain order, the laborers started what
the sheriff described as sporadic"
riots, with disorder breaking out in
spots until the entire camp was in
turmoil. There was no gunplay and
no white persons were injured.


Workers broke up furniture and
used its pieces as clubs to belabor
each other and create further prop
erty damage.


Herbert Spangler, VIA Official in
charge of the camp, withheld COM
ment pending investigation of the
trouble.

MANY fine tributes have been
4'A paid 10 the memory of
Franklin Delano Roosevelt. At
this early date it is impossible
for any one fully to estimate
the benevolent value which the
world has received from the
hands of this noble character.
Many volumes will yet be writ
ten about the life OF this man as
the centuries roll by. For he

whole world.


From the moment Mr.. Roose-

successful conflict against the

happy in the bad years of the
depression. His decisions con-
corning the welfare of the
working man were always fair
and binding. His honest judg-
ment was almost perfect. He
put food in the empty stomachs

terror and fear into the heart

Asiatic despotS. His. tremendous
executive. diplomatic and or
ganizing ability saved the world
from a disastrous chaotic state
which may have lasted for hun
dreds of years. His good work
will remain for all time.


Franklin Delano Roosevelt
was the highest type of states
man that Christian democracy
has yet produced. He was the
ideal democrat that Plato had
visioned when the Greek phi
losopher wrote his immortal
Republic" He was the Pericles
of the modern world. He was
Gladstone and Lincoln rolled
into one. All the political
philosophers are helpless
unless strong. honest, intel
lectual men are found who can
put their fine ideals into force.
Capable leaders like Franklin
Roosevelt are very rare, and
"a long, dark centuries passed
before Plato's ideal appeared
on the political stage.

business executives. President
Truman has already made a
good showing, and he will sur
prise the world in days to come.

text:
Last nights concert by the Buda-
pest Quartet in the Library Of Con-
gress, under the auspices of the
Gertrude Clarke Whittall Founda-
ton, was a refreshing departure
from the regular quartet playing
routine, the group presenting three
outstanding works for a larger en-
semble with the assistance of Milton
Katims, viola, and Daniel Saiden-
berg, cello.


Mozart's Quintet in D Major" for
two violins, two violas and cello.
separated the two sextets on the
program, one by Brahms: "Sextet
in B Flat Major" his first attempt
in this form, characterized by its
sturdy vigor and compactness,
especially when contrasted with
Dvorak's, which closed the concert,
written along simpler lines, reflect
ing national color.


The enjoyable evening was nota-
BILE for the usual freedom of execu-
ton and beauty of tone and more,
because the compositions, especially
the first two on the program, gave
many opportunities for individual
display of style. The opening theme
of Brahms sextet fell to Boris
Kroyt, violist of the Budapest
Quartet, who more than once
showed his sympathetic tone and
led in the rapid spiccato passages
toward the effective finale. Favor
ing the deeper toned instruments
throughout the work, the composer
allotted also several lovely themes
to the cello, the most eloquent being
the one in classic mode where
MiScha Schneiders artistry could
be enjoyed to the fullest.


Listening to the exquisite strains
of Mozart's quintet, written only a
few months before his death, one
could never suspect that under the
polished brilliance and sauve love-
illness of this music lay the tragedy
of dire want which was to carry the
composer to his premature grave.
The adagio of the second move
ment, like a celestial song for the
first violin, scars high above the
other instruments. Supported with
sympathy and understanding by the
rest of the ensemble, Josef Rois-
mann, leader of the organization,
carried the melody with conviction
and refinement.

The War Department has started
an investigation of complaints that
large numbers of its civilian en-
ployes have had their salaries
slashed through indiscriminate job
reclassifications by agency heads, it
was learned today.


The War Department took the
action after numerous complaints
were received from Federal workers
throughout the country. Many
workers have asserted that the
salary increases granted them under
the recently enacted Federal pay
bill have been nullified because their
positions have been down-graded by
their supervisors.


Called Overclassified.


Many of the complaints have been
received from clerks and custodial
workers earning less than $50 a
week. The positions they filled were
considered overclassified by agency
heads and the employees salaries
were cut accordingly, the employees
contended.


A War Department spokesman
said today that 1t was the depart
ment's policy to continually review
all job classifications in accordance
with the intent of the Federal Class
ification Act. However, he said that
many agency heads hestitated to
reclassify jobs during the past few
years since Government employees
generally had not received any wage
boosts and 1t was felt that down.
grading of positions would work
financial hardship on the employees.


However, since passage of the
Federal pay bill, many agency heads
have ordered complete review Of
existing jobs under their supervision
to determine whether persons are
receiving salary rates out of pro-
portion to the jobs they fill.


The department is investigating
the situation to determine whether
some agency heads have been over
jealous in their job classification
review, the official said.


Union Enters Protest.


A sharp protest has been regis
tered by, the United Federal Work.
ers of America (CIO). The union
contended that the wholesale wage
cutting program of the War De-
partment" will nullify for thousands
of employees the effect of the Fed
eral pay raise.


Eleanor Nelson, president of the
UFWA, in a letter to Undersecre-
tary of War Patterson. said the de-
partment's action was contrary to
the intent of Congress when 1t
passed the pay bill. In the bill Con-
gress provided that all workers in
the Federal service should receive
pay raises Of not less than $500.


Wholesale job reclassification will
result in lower living standards for
thousands of Government employees,
who are playing a vital part in the
war effort, Miss Nelson declared.

priation but will consider any pro-
posals submitted.

LAREDO, Tex, Sept. 29.-Twenty

slaughter of 81 men and a woman
are held incommunicado in the
Nuevo Laredo (Mexico) Jail, across
the border from here.


Prosecutor Emilio Villalobos said
last night the men were charged

Texas for farm work and then rob-
bing them of their wages and killing
them on their return to Mexico.


Bodies were found near Browns
vile, Mission and Hidalgo in the
lower Rio Grande during the latter
part of July and August.


American and Mexican Federal
officers have been working on the
case for several weeks.


Mr.. Villalobos said the men will
be tried under an emergency law
which makes the death sentence
mandatory in event a verdict of
guilty Is reached.

took away the radar equipment. The
British followed the same policy re-
garding secret German plants in

thoroughly combed the Zeiss optical
works at Jena before evacuating it
for the Russian occupation.

company, subsidiary of the Bausch
works.


On the north side Of the stadium
the British also found underground
chambers used as storerooms for
aircraft parts. Some intact speci-
mems were left behind by the Rus
slams.

peared, was vital cog in the NaZi
war machine, although 1t was never
made priority target by Allied air
forces. About 80 bombs fell in the
area during the war, but they were
spillovers from other objectives.


At least feet of concrete pro-
tected the top story of the under
ground tunnels where the various
war activities were carried on.


The Berlin radio maintained an
emergency transmitter and studio
underground in the beautifully land
scaped Olympic village that Adolf
Hitler built to house the worlds

LONDON. Dec. 30 (UP)-
Russian armored divisions broke
across the Hron River barrier and
drove west through the Danube
Valley toward Bradshaw and
Vienna today while in Budapest
thousands of Nazi and Hungarian
troops fought on for the fifth
straight day In a suicidal battle
to delay the Red Army invasion
of Austria.


With major elements of their
Second and Third Ukrainian
armies still pinned down in the
struggle for Budapest, the Soviet
advance south Of the Danube ap-
peared to have been stalled mo-
mentarily about 80 miles from
Vienna, where the Germans were
making a determined stand on the
edge Of the Gyor Plain.


REINFORCEMENTs ARRIVE


The Moscow morning eommuni-
que made no mention of fighting
along the 55-mile front from the
Danube south to Lake Balaton,
but Berlin said the Russians were
reinforcing their lines after being
stopped by strong German coun-
terattacks.


To the north, however, the Rus
slams hurdled the Hron barrier
near its confluence with the DAN
ube and shook their armor loose
on the Bradshaw plain after a
savage, two-day battle that cost
the Germans 1000 casualties and
as tanks.


RIVER BARRIER CROSSED


The Hron. second of the six
Danube tributaries covering the
eastern approaches to Vienna, was
forced by Red forces yesterday
with the capture of the west bank
towns of Mana and Parkan, II
miles southeast of Bratislava and
little more than 100 miles from
Vienna.


Inside Budapest, meanwhile,
one of the wars bloodiest street
battles ragged on through its fifth
day. Spanked by a fanatical core
of NaZi Elite Guards. the Axis
garrison was fighting until death
for partially ruined city that
the German high command itself
callously wrote off as of no
further military value except
that its prolonged defense might
delay the Soviet march on
Austria.

Meyer said in addition to

mass of evidence accumulated for
use against them was SO great the
ordinary legal processes could not
handle the cases Immediately.


Quisling's case has been post
poned, Meyer said, until a legal

delay was taken under an extraor-
binary wartime act of the Nor
wegian government in exile that
superseded the normal 24-hour ar
raignment rule. The police head
said Quisling followers who had fed
to Sweden were being held in spe-
cial camps and would be returned
to Norway for trial as facilities per-
mitted.


Quisling himself, arrested Tues
day, is being held in the Oslo Jail
as common prisoner without priv
ileges.


German troops completed the

line last midnight and today were in
disarmament centers outside the
city. The only uniformed Germans
still within the city were naval per-
sonnel ordered by the Allied Con-

Parliament yesterday that King

encourage in 1910 and accused the
exiled monarch of having declared

chouwer for the Catholic (pro-Leo-
pold) party. Spaak reviewed the 1910

render in mind early in the cam

"and most painful interview with

night of May 24-25, 1910. He said the

monarch from abroad.

point: The Allied cause is lost.
France is beaten. England will only
continue the struggle in her do
minions and colonies. Belgiums
part in this war has come to an
end. We can only hope for an in

The Foreign Minister said the
cabinet two days later sent the King
a message urging him to throw pro-

liar messages were sent in 1912 and
in 1943.

reached the sovereign, who ignored
the first two and did not answer the
last until after Belgium's liberation,
when he demanded solemn and
complete apology" for the cabinets
attitude toward the King.

yes, most of them were marched

pletely satisfying Russian demands. :"

terfuge worked well because "the
Russians carried out their deliveries,
as planned, right up to the start of

ber, 1910. seven months before the
attack.


The Office Immediately prepared

casian oil fields. power plants and

BALTIMORE, May 22.-The Coast
Guard said yesterday that a young
man and woman probably were
drowned over the week end when
their small sailing skiff capsized in
Chesapeake Bay.


The overturned boat was found
floating about 6 miles from Love
Point. The Baltimore Coast Guard
Office identified the missing couple
as Randolph Dashiell, 81, of Rich
mond, Va, who had been staying in
Baltimore, and Miss Jane Hoffman,
Baltimore.


Relatives and friends of the pair
told Coast Guard officers they left
a point near Back River Friday
afternoon, expecting to be gone but
a few hours.


Coast Guardsmen who recovered
the skiff the next day said that
there had been a violent windstorm
over that section of the Bay Friday
night. They said they believed that
the boat had capsized.

An American actress who had

The nervous strain and hard work

But what a day that was," ex-

when the first Yankee jeep hit

Mrs. Tartiere, native of Kenosha, !,

Her tensest moments came last

pathway for the advancing troops.
Many Allied airmen parachuted
from crippled planes in the fields
and forests around Barbizon. But
the underground, after long prac-
tice, was functioning smoothly.


A neighbor hurried into Mrs.
Tartiere's home to say a "big red

tree behind her home.


Mrs. Tartiere grabbed up a mar
ket basket, donned a cloak and
strolled over.


For Heavens sake, where are

The American woman wrote

Mrs. Tartiere, she told reporters in

INTO the car with some extra cloth
ing, and they drove to the place in
the forest. Both flyers had been
badly burned, one had broken leg
and the others lower lip was hang
ng open from deep laceration.


Wounded Don't Bat Eye.


They threw trench coats over the
pair and helped them into the car.
A German guard stopped them while
they were returning.


Neither of the wounded boys bat

Il pretended I was alighting to |

month that elapsed before American

There is music in the meadows
these sunny, stirring days.
The bobolinks dash about repeating
their name for all the world to
hear; the song sparrows sit on the
fence posts and send their caroling
arias over the daisy and buttercup
dotted green-grass carpet. The barn
swallows swoop and circle, dip and
climb as they gather insects for the
hungry babies in the mud-plaster
nests against the barn rafters.


Along the brush-lined creek that
meanders through the meadow, the
vireos and warblers are building
their homes for the summer. Per-
haps it would be more accurate to
say that the ladies are doing the
work and their mates are telling
the world that all is we'll. From the
edge of the meadow in those sections
he frequents that gorgeous, orr
entail potentate, the ring
pheasant, occasionally sends his
hoarSe challenge across the field
while his drably-brown. demure
mate sits on the clutch of eggs hid
den in the brush and grass.


One who is attuned to the music
OF the land can hear other songs,
quiet, steady music that forms a
background for the solo selections.
The breeze moves the grasses and
flowers and plays soft. appealing
melody. There are the faint chirp-
ings of countless insects as they go
about the days living Over all is
the steady hum of bees as they go
from flower to flower. 1t is the time
when the soul-filling symphony of
natures orchestra is in It's hest
form. Meadow melodies are not
crashing. martial tunes. They are
the Joyous, soft songs of wild life
when the miracle of birth is swing
ing through its appointed cycle.
Meadow melodies are songs of peace
and contentment.

watched in horror, a jealousy
crazed former marine early today
shot and killed his estranged wife
as she left a gay Lake st. Clair
tavern with two Selfridge Field
soldiers.


The victim was Mrs. Andrew
Cremers, 23, of Richmond. Held
as her slayer is the husband, An
drew Cremers, %. Macomb

charged that Cremers trailed his
wife to the night club and then

emerged from a side entrance

Arrested Immediately and taken
10 Mt. Clemens Jail, Cremers was

can. She deserved IL"

mers had been stalking his wife

Last night, Mrs. Cremers and
some friends went 10 NaH,S-oR-the-

half mile from the main gate
of Selfridge Field


TRIES TO GRAB GUN


For several hours. according TO
the sheriff, Mrs. Cremers and her
party danced there. All the while,
the sheriff continued. Cremers
was outside brooding about the
threatened divorce.


When Mrs. Cremers emerged
into the moonlight, laughing and
chatting with her sister. Mrs.
Rena Carroll, and the soldiers,
Cremers approached carrying the
gun.


Mrs. Cremers reached out and
grabbed the barrel of the gun,
the sheriff said, but she was too
late. Cremers pulled the trigger
twice, the sheriff said, and then
fired three more bullets into his
wife after she had slumped TO the
ground.


One bullet went through her
left shoulder, three into her heart
and one into her right side


'CRAZED BY JEALOUSY


While his wife lay dead and
stunned witnesses Of the Staying
stood around, Cremers said:


II guess was just crazy jeal-
Gus OF her. I had told her to
stay away from soldiers and
when 1 saw her tonight 1 must
have gone crazy"


A husky man, weighing more
than 200 pounds, Cremers joined
the marines Nov. II. 1943. He
was sent 10 the south Pacific.


While in Hawaii he contracted
tropical fever.


After long stay in a hospital
there, he was sent back TO the
marine hospital in Corona, Cal,
and then discharged.


The Cremers had been married
seven years.


Sheriff Ensign said CrenerS had
recently obtained employment at
the Bundy Tubing Corp.


He was held for investigation of
murder.

Washington and Alexandria and

Ball Park tomorrow and Sunday.

devoting window display space to

Sunday.

Shetland sheepdogs lead. Since the
national speciality show of the breed
is being held in conjunction with

schnauzers and bulldogs.

corners. In addition, doughnuts and
apples will be sold by pretty girls.

added to the hospitals funds.

The submarine Salmon attacked

Depth charges so injured the Sal

The submarines crew manned her
deck gun and fought with such
ferocity that the Jap ships were
driven off. But the Salmon was
left near a welter of Japanese

lection.

Marianas in his Play Navy Liber-
ator Seven hundred miles from
home, 1t. Box sighted an Emily
Navy nickname for the Jap A.
engined Flying Boat, headed for

1t. Box already had flown to the

home. Ignoring the warning Of his
fuel gauge, he attacked the Emily,
and chased her $50 miles back

of them began to trail fire, and the

miles an hour.

And thus gained a position 1000
feet behind and above the Jap. His
bow gunner fired into the Emily,
silencing its deck turret and blast
ing the plexiglass dome and its
Imooring.


The Jap banked, almost standing
on its wing tip, with one engine
smoking. While the Jap tried to
bring his guns to bear, 1t. Thomp-
sons gunners poured slugs into his
engines and wings.


=, 1t. Thompson forced his huge
craft into violent turn at 200 feet
altitude and overlook the Jap. The
Emily, now only so feet above the
water, began to jettison gear and
bombs.


Foe Drops Into Sea. |


He dropped his own cargo of
depth charges to tighten the plane
and dropped slightly behind the
faltering Emily. The Jap's wing
tip dropped and touched the water,
ripping off the entire wing. I'm
mediately the hull slammed into the
sea and exploded.


Thus guarded by patrols from

MEXICO CITY (P).-Manuel Avila
Camacho started his sixth and last year
as President of Mexico yesterday with
one of his most troublesome problems
ahead of him.


He has promised the country honest
elections" when Mexico votes next July
7 for his successor. But his party, the
government party, PRM (Partido Revo-
lucionario Mexicano), last week declared
against important election reforms.


Aside from that problem, Avila Ca
the one of steering Mexico away from
too much revolution" and in doing
so he has accumulated much credit for
progress.


Probably the war did more than any
thing else to help the President steer
his course. The United States aided his
program with experts and money be-
cause it was interested in buying Mex
lean raw materials.


Mexico declared war against Ger
many, Italy and Japan, June /, 1912, but
for some time before that Mexico was
preparing to be a war factory for the
United States. She did not send any
military units to Europe but many SOL
diers of Mexican blood were at the front
and some won the Congressional Medal
of Honor.


Germany bought and sold much here
before the war, many Germans lived
here and many Mexicans were sympa-
thetic to Germany-so Avila Camacho
is given credit by his friends with
certain achievement in putting Mexico
frankly into the war on the Allied side.
Two typical accomplishments of the
President are his campaign to make
every Mexican literate and his fostering
of industry.


People speak and usually think Of the
President as mild, neutral and not
strong. They seem surprised when they
tabulate the Presidents remaking of
Mexico, still incomplete, but well started.
The President is the persuasive type.
He usually speaks only when his back
stage work has swung enough people
into line.


Since December 1, 1910, Avila Ca
macho has given the country broad
social security system, nearing its sec
ond year; a stronger financial system,
|eone-year military service, projected be-
fore Mexico entered the war; much
basic industrial development, better
roads, a stable judiciary, and the United
States-Mexico water treaty, ratified lat
month, which shares the Rio Grc !.
and other border waters for tremendous
future irrigation.

CHUNGKING, Aug. IA. - The
grave situation between the Centra,
Government and Northern Commu.
nists now precludes the possibility
of Generalissimo Chang Kai-shek
representing China at any japanese
surrender ceremony, it became
known today.


An authoritative source reported
the Chinese delegation would be
headed by Gen. Hsu Yung-chang
chief Of the board Of military oper-
ations in Chungking since 1898
Previously it had been reported
Chang would lead the Chinese dele
gates.


The Communists, headed by Gen
Chu Ten, with headquarters at
Yenan, were reported to be moving
toward Shanghai and Nanking, key
coastal cities, without which the
national governments position
would be seriously weakened.


To offset any move by the Com
munist to gain quick control of the
ports with their immense stores of
Japanese arms and ammunitions
the central government was re-
ported ready to fly veteran Chinese
air-borne troops into the cities the
moment Japan signs the surrender
terms.


Some Japanese units, front-line
dispatches said, have ceased fighting
southeast of Shanghai and are
negotiating for their capitulation
Chu Teh has urged Koreans forced
into the Japanese Army to desert
and come over to the Communist
forces with their arms.

The War Department has started
an investigation of complaints that
large numbers of its civilian en-
ployes have had their salaries
slashed through indiscriminate job
reclassifications by agency heads, it
was learned today.


The War Department took the
action after numerous complaints
were received from Federal workers
throughout the country. Many
workers have asserted that the
salary increases granted them under
the recently enacted Federal pay
bill have been nullified because their
positions have been down-graded by
their supervisors.


Called Overclassified.


Many of the complaints have been
received from clerks and custodial
workers earning less than $50 a
week. The positions they filled were
considered overclassified by agency
heads and the employees salaries
were cut accordingly, the employees
contended.


A War Department spokesman
said today that 1t was the depart
ment's policy to continually review
all job classifications in accordance
with the intent of the Federal Class
ification Act. However. he said that
many agency heads hestitated to
reclassify jobs during the past few
years since Government employees
generally had not received any wage
boosts and 1t was felt that down.
grading of positions would work
financial hardship on the employees.


However, since passage of the
Federal pay bill, many agency heads
have ordered complete review of
existing jobs under their supervision
to determine whether persons are
receiving salary rates out of pro-
portion to the jobs they fill.


The department is investigating
the situation to determine whether
some agency heads have been over
jealous in their job classification
review, lie official said.


,Un.cn Enters Protest.


A sharp protest has been regis
tered by the United Federal Work.
ers of America (CIO). The union
contended that the wholesale wage
cutting program of the War De-
partment" will nullify for thousands
of employees the effect of the Fed

UFWA, in a letter to Undersecre-
tary of War Patterson, said the de-
partment's action was contrary to
the intent of Congress when 1t
passed the pay bill. In the bill Con-
gress provided that all workers in
the Federal service should receive
pay raises of not less than $500.


Wholesale job reclassification will
result In lower living standards for
thousands of Government employees,

A declaration that the Washing
ton National Airport should be q
part Of the District, instead of Vir-
ginia, came today from Senator Nc
Carran, Democrat, of Nevada, chair
man Of the Senate Judiciary Com
mittee.


Shortly after Chairman Randolph
of the House District Committee
yesterday reintroduced his bill Of
last session to settle the century,
old District Virginia boundary dis
pute, the Nevada Senator expressed
hope the issue would be settled, but
added the airport should not be
ceded to Virginia.


During the past Congress, Sena-
tor McCarran sponsored two bills
seeking to end confusion arising
from uncertainty of the old bound
ary line, which has created a mo
mans land" along the Virginia side
Of the Potomac.


One would have declared the air.
port in the District, though other
wise fixing the boundary at the
present mean highwater mark on
the Virginia shore, as does the Ran
dolph bill. The latter bill, however,
leaves the port within Virginia ter
ritory and, since it is federally
owned, reserves to the United States
concurrent jurisdiction over the air
port.


Senator McCarran, seeing little
chance of action on his boundary
bill last session, also offered a bill
to apply District laws and regula-
tions to all the Federal reservations
in nearby Virginia without touch
ing the boundary issue. That bill
also died with the old Congress.
Meanwhile, House District Com
mittee spokesmen said the Air
Transport Association, representing
81 operating air lines, had suggested
an amendment to the Randolph bill
which would treat the airport as
an exclusive Federal jurisdiction,
though granting Virginia limited
taxing power and powers of serving
criminal and civil processes there.

Associated Press War Correspondent.


MOSCOW, April 25.-A fam
tastic battle surged through the
subways beneath Berlin's rubble-
strewn streets today as Russian
forces fought to crush fanatical
Nazi troops using the under
ground network to stage surprise
raids on Soviet communications


Eyewitness accounts sent by Rus
sian correspondents from the Ger
man capital said Nazi soldiers, rush.
ing from station to station in ex-
press trains, were constantly pop
ping up at unexpected spots behind
Red Army troops fighting their way
toward the center of the city


These and other reports of the
struggle raging inside Berlin sug-
gested the Germans might succeed
in making a long defense of theif
capital.


A Red Star correspondent, de-
scribing the strategic use to which
the Germans were putting the Ber-
lin subways, declared the battle for
the city was assuming "a peculiar
character"


1T is difficult to define" he wrote
Firing is going on UP ahead and
then there are unexpected battles in
the comparatively deep rear.


THE Germans have transferred
from the center of Berlin through
the subways many fresh units. They
crawl from the subway stations,
bringing field pieces with them. The
streets are again under fire.


I'VE have to wipe them out or
drive them back into the tunnels,
otherwise they would spread over
many blocks and seriously threaten
our communications


The Red Star correspondent told
of fierce hour-long battle around
one station where the Nazis sud-
denly appeared in an area from
which they previously had been
cleared.


Russian tanks and artillery finally
were called into action to blast a
path for Soviet infantry, who drove
the Germans back into the subway
at bayonet point and then followed
them in the pitch-dark tunnel to
set off mines and seal it up.


"Our artillery even managed to
pull in small guns and fire along the
tunnels" the correspondent said.


Red Air Force pilots reported
roads leading into the city from the
west crowded with traffic. apparent
ly reserves hurrying in from previ-
GUS positions before the Americans
along the Elbe.


This traffic, however, was running
a gauntlet of bursting shells and
bombing and strafing from Russian
and British planes.


Reds Hold 27 Suburbs.


BY this morning, Russian forces
steadily fighting their way toward
the center of Berlin held q suburbs
and intermediate sections of the
city and at least eight railway and
electric railway stations, including
some of the largest. Pilots said they
could see new large fires in the city


The Izvestia correspondent in Ber-
lin described the center of the cap
ital as an inferno"


White flags are appearing in
larger numbers in the streets down
which the Russians are driving,
these advices said. Nazi officers
were reported shooting down men
in other places if they tried to re-
treat or give up.


Water, gas, electricity and food
are giving out in the city. Russian
shells have burst many water mains.
A major gas works and a substation
have been captured. Some power
stations have been damaged and
many electric wires are down. Tele-
phone communications are disrupted.


Continuous Counterattacks.


The Hitlerites are launching
continuous counterattacks, but So

LONDON, Oct. 17.-Last nights
announcement that Pan American
Always will provide a roundtrip
across the Atlantic for about $500.
beginning Saturday, has greatly
shocked London.


AS recently as October IL, Ivor
Thomas, parliamentary secretary
for civil aviation, optimistically told

would hold its own with American
civil aviation, once it got going.


Now. air correspondents of London
newspapers are drawing attention to
the fact that British civil aviation
will not even be on a competitive
basis with American in trans-Atlan-
tic trade during the foreseeable
future.


The British Overseas Always
Corp. charges about $572 for one
way trip across the Atlantic in sum-
mertime, and on the eastbound trip,
an additional American tax of Is
per cent is charged.


During the winter season, which
is Just beginning, its ships make
the crossing via the Azores and
Bermuda and the fare is increased,
the westbound trip costing $792 and
The eastbound trip 81 ,292.


Pan American will start its service
with roomy, speedy Douglas Lock
heed Consultations.


The British Overseas Always
Corp. uses slow-fiying boats and the
12-passenger land machines it has
ordered will not be ready for months.

ANNAPOLIS, Md, Dec, Ed
ward F. Hotter of Middletown was
elected master of the Maryland
State Grange yesterday as the farm
group concluded it's 73d annual con-
vention here.


Mr.. Hotter, former Grange secre-
tary, succeeds T. Roy BrookeS, Bel
Air. Guy S. Meloy, Lanham, was

eminent subsidies to agriculture.

ers to accept farm jobs without sur

The fact that Switzerland is act
ing as intermediary in the negotia-
tions for Japan's surrender empha-
sizes the role that little land-locked
country has played throughout
World War Two, not merely in diplo-
macy but also in every sort of inter-
belligerent activity. Thereby, Swift
zerland has carried on it's peculiar
international status - that of' the
worlds unique professional neu-
trail"


The germ of Swiss neutrality runs
back centuries. Toward the close of
the Middle Ages the inhabitants of
Europe's mountain core, the Alps,
banded together for their mutual
protection against all external enc
mics and this confederation, though
formed of units with different Ian
guages and cultures. proved strong
enough to survive the shock of
the Reformation which divided the
Swiss on religious lines. The con-
federation thus escaped the reli-
giouS wars which desolated both
France and Germany. and it's inde-
pendence was acknowledged by the
general European settlement of
Westphalia in 1648. This acknowl-
edgment reflected the widespread
realization that Swiss aloofneSS
from the game of power politics was
best for European stability. There
after, Swiss neutrality was attacked
only once, when Napoleon incorpo-
rated the little country in his short
lived empire. Atonement was made
by the Vienna Congress which set
the pattern for the European con-
tinent that subsisted basically down
to World War One, century later.
BY the Vienna settlement, Switzer-
land was formally dedicated to per-
manent neutrality.


That acknowledged status gave
the Swiss the opportunity of playing
benefcent role as the seat of in
ternational institutions like the Red
Cross and as honest broker" be-
tween belligerents in wartime, when
Switzerland provides meeting
ground and clearing house for mat
ters like exchanges of prisoners and
indirect diplomatic intercourse. 1t
likewise rendered Geneva the logical
site for the League of Nations.


During World War Two, Switzer-
land has done it's utmost to fulfill
the neutral function which has be-
come the ideal of its people, and has
resolutely maintained its neutral
status despite heavy economic pres
sure. The task has been harder
than in World War One, because the
very concept of neutrality by any
nation has been sharply assailed as
rendered obsolete by the changed
conditions in world affairs. Never
theless, Switzerland carries on it's
national tradition and is making
another useful contribution by its
present role as diplomatic liaison
between Japan and the Allies.
headline: Swiss Neutral Role

LONDON, Dec. 24.-All prepara-
tions had been completed today for
the formal opening early next year
of the United Nations Organization
blueprinted by the San Francisco
Conference and embodying the
worlds hopes for peace.


With adjournment of the Prepar-
story Commission yesterday, the
path was cleared for official opening
of UNO when its first general as
sembly convenes here January 10.
The assembly will have to elect nom
permanent members OF the Security
Council, Economic and Social Coun-
Gil, Trusteeship Council and a sec
retary general before UNO can get
into full swing.


Among the several tough politi-
cal issues to come before the first
meeting will be the atomic bomb.
American and British representa-
tives here say they still intend to
put before the assembly plans for
an international commission along
lines suggested by President Tru-
man, British Prime Minister Attlee
and Canadian Prime Minister Mac
kenzie King.


Anglo American spokesman say
they will avoid discussion of what
should be done with the bomb and
concentrate discussion on construc-
tive uses of atomic energy, with
regulation Of its destructive uses.


However, other delegates have
made 1t clear that once the atom
Is up for discussion, they will air
all their views on its place in in
ternational society.


Several smaller powers have served
notice they will continue their battle
against preponderance of the Big
Five in UNO.


The assembly also must pick the
exact location of UNO's permanent
home. The Preparatory Commission
decided only that it should be on
the East Coast of the United States.
An interim committee will visit the
United States and narrow the can
didates down to maximum of six
cities, from which the Assembly will
choose one.

The AuStrians have voted. They
had their hearts in it, for more than
go per cent of the registered voters
went to the pollS-a majority of
them women. The elections were
undoubtedly unhampered. so the
result represents the genuine will of
the Austrian people.


That result confirms the predic-
tions of most qualified foreign OBJ
servers. The Conservative Peoples
party apparently is the big winner.
Next comes the Socialists, the politi-
cal heir of the Christian Socialists
before Austria was absorbed in the
Third Reich. At the tail end come
the Communists, with less than 10
per cent of the vote.


This overall picture requires some
analysis to get the detailed outlook.
The basic fact about Austria is that
it is a small country containing an
abnormally large capital city, Vienna
and its metropolitan suburbs con-
tanning nearly one-third the total
population. This is hangover from
the days when Vienna was the head
of great empire which went to
pieces at the close of World War I.
The working masses of Vienna have
been traditionally Socialist, and this
trend is echoed in the smaller indus
trial centers. But the rural popula-
tion everywhere has been equally
conservative and clerical in its po-
litical allegiance. Thus, Austria has
always been sharply split between
city and country in its political and
economic ideals. The one political
element that has been eliminated
by the war is the faction favoring
amalgamation with Germany. That
faction, historically known as Pan
Germans, became Nazis after the
rise of. Hitler and have now been
virtually eliminated with the ruin
of the Third Reich.


On the other hand. Communism,
which never appealed to the individ-
ualistic and relatively undisciplined
Austrians, has apparently been given
a further setback by the harshnessl
and excesses Of the Red Army since
Russian occupation.


With both extremes eliminated,
the political picture is a simplified
version of that in the 1890 parlia-
mentary elections, held before the
rise of Hitlerism. At that time the
Socialists polled A per cent Of the
total vote. the Christian Socialists
40 per cent. while the Pan-Germans
and other minor groups got 16 per
cent. The present outcome gives
the Peoples party clear majority

istas and the powerful Socialist
party-itself vigorous opponent
of Peron.

turned her proud, tough old nose into
the wind at full throttle-she had come

The japanese fleet had split and was

To the U. S. S. Enterprise, sole sur

presidential unit citation, 1t was an
old story. She has a habit of casting
a shadow across "the rising sun
Way back in Al, returning from Wake

japanese sneak attack and hers were
the only carrier-based aircraft in action
that December 7. Since then the 19,50O-

Trails of Her Enemy Hunts


On map the trail of her persistent
hunts for the enemy looks like the
scribblings in a childs picture book,
and takes in most of the major Pacific
engagements.


She sailed deep into the Marshalls
and Gilberts soon after Pearl Harbor
for the first American blows against
enemy territory.


She escorted the Hornet to within
300 miles of Tokyo for Jimmy Doolittle's
daring air raid.


Often she hunted alone, for there
was a time when Uncle Sam could
muster no other carrier for the battle
When the sleek new carriers arrived
she refused to be benched.


She was in on the invasion of the
Gilberts and Marshalls, at Truk. Palau,
zap, Woleai and Ulithi in the Caro-
lines; Jaluit in the Marshalls, Emirau
in the South Pacific, Hollandia in New
Guinea, Saipan, Guam, the Bonins.
the Ryukyus, Formosa and the Philip
pines.


Saved Fleet From Attack


In the Gilberts she pioneered with
night combat fighters, losing one of
her most famous flyers, 1t. Commander
E. H. (Butch) O'Hare, but the venture
saved the American feet from the
largest co-ordinated night air attack
every launched against it.


In the battle of the Philippines Sea
in June, 1914, one of her planes was
first to sight the enemy fleet, and later

cupola.

mates during the early morning

prisoners were reported wounded.

not clear. but it has been known
generally that the prison was over
crowded and sanitary conditions
were bad Regina Coeli has been
used by the present government, as
it was by the Fascists, to house both
criminals and political prisoners.

LONDON.-A German soldier crouch
ing in a wooded shelter in Holland
pressed a button and seconds later,
without warning, death came to London
200 miles across the North Sea.


Men were killed at their desks. Women
went out to buy the days groceries and
never returned. A house was a home one
minute and pile of rubble the next


People in quiet places all over the
world read the stories and looked SYM
pathetically at pictures of what Hitler's
W. rockets did to London. But stories
awful eeriness and suspense of living
here through those 20l nightmarish
days of the rocket war.


The 6ying bombs were terrifying and
would kill you just as quickly-but you
could hear them coming and had
sporting chance of ducking.


Death Without Warning


The final rocket ordeal was the most
fantastic episode of the war.


A deadly robot monster weighing Is
tons, launched from small, camoutiaged
sites hundreds of miles away and trav-
cling through the stratosphere at a
speed faster than sound, would descend
without warning, killing, manning and
destroying. Never before had civilian
population been subjected to such
ruthless and savage assault.


Hitler and his clever scientists hoped
to terrorize the people of this country
into a negotiated peace. Fire and fury
had been rained down on them from
the start. Their nerves were frayed and
their bodies tired, but their stubborn
courage never failed. They thumbed
their noses at Jerry and carried on. No
one here will deny, however, that had
D day not come when it did London
. might easily have become the raging
volcano" that DR.. Goebbles had so ex-
ultantly described.


At intervals throughout the day and
night the customary noises Of big city
were punctuated with the thud and
roar of exploding rockets.


The Va explosion was unlike anything
before-a deafening crack followed by
a disintegrating roar as the blast tore
down buildings and the earth trembled.
But eventually the explosions attracted
little attention unless they were very
close.

Officials of Federal employees
unions here today expressed their
preference for the Kilgore bill
which provides unemployment COM
pensation benefits for Government
workers during the reconversion
period, over a similar type of legis-
lation introduced in the House by
Chairman Doughton of the House
Ways and Means Committee.


The union leaders feel that the
legislation introduced by Senator
Kilgore, Democrat, of West Vir-
ginia provides vastly better benefits
for Federal workers than does the
Doughton bill.


For one thing, the Kilgore bill
places all Federal employees under
standard system, similar to the
Districts unemployment compensa-
ton plan. This would pay a Gov
ernment worker who lost his job in
the reconversion period up to 66 per
cent of his earnings in a 13-week
base period taken from the year
Immediately preceding dismissal.
Maximum payment would be $25
and would continue for 26 weeks Of
any calendar year.


States Can Reject Plan.


In contrast, the Doughton bill
provides for unemployment COM
pensation benefits based on the
standards of the particular State
where a Federal worker is employed.
Since most States unemployment
compensation benefits are consider
ably less than 66 per cent of an
employees highest weekly earning,
this would mean less jobless COM
pensation benefits for many Gov
ernment workers working outside
Washington.


Both bills would supplement State
unemployment funds with Federal
money to bring jobless payments to
two-thirdS of a workers previous
with a $25 maximum, but
the various States have the right to
reject the plan.


The union officials also pointed
out that the Kilgore measure, in
contrast to the Doughton bill, pro-
vides transportation funds for un-
workers who get jobs in
other cities Both bills, however,
fail to meet the unions demands for
transportation funds to return Gov
eminent workers to their homes
after the war.


Another objection the union Of
ficials have to the Doughton bill is
the provision that the measure
would not go into effect until 600,-
900 persons throughout the country
are receiving unemployment COM
pensation benefits.


Backs Kilgore Bill.


The United Federal Workers Of
America (CIO) estimated that un-
der this provision actual unemploy-
ment of more than 100000 people
would have to exist before Govern
ment employees would gain any bene-
fits. This was explained by the fact
that the 100000 would not nearly
represent all those unemployed,
since large groups Of workers, in
Guiding Federal employees, have
never been covered by unemploy-
ment compensation benefits and
therefore would not be reported as
unemployed.


The American Federation of Gov
eminent Employees (AFL) also has
announced its support of the Kill
gore bill william Green, president
Of the AFL, has indorsed the prin-
ciples of the measure.


The National Federation of Fed
eral Employees also has expressed
approval of the Kilgore bill, al
though the union said passage of
the Doughton bill also would be ac-
ceptable.


Both bills were introduced after
President Truman requested legisla-
ton to cushion the shock of unem-
ployment during the reconversion
period.

MANILA, Sunday, May 13.-The
big Japanese Del Monte airdrome
in North Central Mindanao, Philip

American 10th Division Friday, Gen.
Macarthur announced today, after
the Yanks made a 14-mile advance
from their invasion beachhead.


Elements of Maj. Gen. Rapp
Brush's division, which landed at
Macajalar Bay Thursday and ad-
vanced four miles the first day,
pushed south along Sayre Highway,
taking the Alae road junction and
reaching point 60 miles from the

Skillful air support made the

Japs Developed Airfield.


Del Monte is the site of the big

Maramag Airfield was secured by

the Japanese into the hills between
the Talomo and Davao Rivers.


Yank and guerrilla forces fight

Mia watershed in East Central Lu-
zon are within miles of closing
their pincers on Japanese forces in
the vicinity of Ipo Dam.


Naval units patrolling the east

bombers and fighters plastered all

island with $50 tons of explosives.

stallations and shipping around

pine-based bombers and fighters,

Railways and rolling stock also

japanese airf1elds near Canton

Of bombs.


Shipping and rail lines from
Shanghai south into French Indo-
China, where the vital japanese

aerial sweeps included two freight
ers left afire off Formosa, a 1,000-ton

japanese base on the New Guinea

commander of the 5th Air Force,
expressed belief that repeated at
tacks on Saigon had practically put
that former French naval base out
of commission. 1t had been used
by the japanese as shipping re-
pair base.

tower.

ners and other personnel trapped

in IL minutes.

disrupted and damage was done In
other departments, the ship made
temporary repairs while still under
way and carried out her assignment
at Lingayen.

President Roosevelt died from
what doctors call cerebral hemor-
rhage. which means a sudden ex-
tensive bleeding in the brain due
to a ruptured blood vessel.


Nonmedical people recognize a
cerebral hemorrhage under other
names such as stroke, or a stroke
Of apoplexy.


This is usually what happens in
a case like this:


AS people grow old their arteries
lose their elasticity. They become
hard, brittle. Usually, with advanc-
ing age blood pressure increases.


Some arteries in the brain grow
harder and more brittle than blood
vessels in other parts of the body.


Then, usually without warning, a
blood vessel in the brain gives way.
Blood pours through the brain,
paralyzing nerve centers.


Very often people get a mild
hemorrhage and recover and then
maybe much later get second, final
stroke which kills. Medical men
say the hemorrhage which killed
the President must have been very
severe.

ing forces reached the infamous Ca
banatuan prisoner pens on Luzon,

able conditions subsequently dis

Il capacity for torture, savagry and

Railroad and bus station ticket

for holiday rush, sat back and
took it easy with most other peo-
pie yesterday in the most surpris-
ing development of the Fourth of
July.


Usually thronged Union Station
was morgue in contrast with
normal wartime days, and bus travel
was below par, a paradox trans
portation officials attributed to two
factors: %, most holidayites out
smarted" the conditions that pre-
vail by travelling last week end,
and (2), others outsmarted them
selves by remaining at home in
anticipation of rush.


Then there were those who took
patriotism and the ONCE of De-
fense Transportation seriously and
decided to give servicemen prior
ity on furlough travel


Those who sell tickets answer
questions and handle baggage be-
gan paying for their respite early
however. BY 10 O'Clock last night
an influx of travellers who left the
District early to beat the rush
brought traffic back to normal at
Union Station.


Bus Terminal Congested.


The Greyhound Lines terminal,
which yesterday reported one of the
lightest days in two years, began
handling turn away ticket lines
last night. The Annapolis Wash
ington route was particularly con-
gested and many servicemen were
left stranded, company officials said.


Philadelphia and New York-bound
travellers. accustomed to jockeying
for positions at Union Station ticket
windows and gates, were pleasantly
shocked by prewartime freedom
of movement. Seats were available
on almost any train at almost any
time of the day and many passen-
gers enjoyed the luxury of seat
to themselves.


Even dining cars going out of
Washington, usually incomplete
these days without a two or three
hour waiting line. were easily ac-
cessible on most trains.


Crowded beaches in the Wash
ington. Annapolis and Baltimore
areas furnished added evidence that
the exodus took place over the week
end by those seeking relief from
the heat. The American Automo-
bile Association reported heavy
highway traffic by motorists who
had saved gas coupons for the oc-
casion. Many were said to be turned
away at jammed Beverly Beach.


Rushing Business In Norfolk Area.


Beach resorts in the Norfolk (Va)
area did a rushing business, but
only the Pennsylvania Central Air
Lines reported capacity holiday
traffic. Buslines, steamship COM
panies and railroads found travel
lighter than last week end. and ex-
pected another surge this week end.


Officials at Virginia Beach and
Ocean View reported hotels and
cottages filled to capacity, but the
beaches were sparsely populated
compared to last Saturday and
Sunday when the mercury scared
to 100 degrees.


Surprisingly light traffic was re-
corded between Norfolk and Vir-
ginia Beach, an indication that
many yacatiopers who arrived last
week end were making a week OF
it, transportation men said.

TINIAN, Marianas Islands, July
i1.-Thermal air currents generated
by fires B-29s started in Wakayama
yesterday were so strong they showed
the incendiaries right back into one
Super Fort through its own bomb
bay.


Maj. Robert H. Langdale of
Houston, Tex, said today that just
after his bombardier had released
all incendiaries, fused and ready to
burst into flame, the hot air sent
them crashing upward into his
B-29. They tore away a bomb bay
door and hit the planes horizontal
stabilizer, but fell out again without
doing any major damage to the
plane.


Climaxing the weird experience,
powerful updrafts of scorching hot
air tipped the Super Fort over on
its back in a half loop heading the
plane back over the burning target.


The plane was flying belly up for
several seconds until Maj. Langdale
brought it under control and back on
its course for safe return to Tinian

NEW BRUNSWICK, N. j., Oct
22.-Two Rutgers University sopho-
mores and young woman guest
died of suffocation, and another
young woman guest, four students
and a colored houseman were in
jured early yesterday when three
alarm fire swept the three-story fra
ternity house leased by Sigma AL
pha Mu


The dead were Raymond Berger,
10, Jersey City, and Benjamin Cor
don, Trenton, Rutgers students, and
Miss Joyce Patricia Katzman, 20
Teaneck, former student at the
New jersey College for Women, who
transferred to New York Univer-
sity.


Middlesex County Coroner Robert
H. Jamison said the three died of
suffocation in the $4,000 fire which
wrecked the 35-year-old fraternity
house. The four Rutgers men and
the other woman guest were in
tured leaping from second-story
windows. The houseman, who slept
on the ground floor, also was hurt.


Raymand Schiff, 10, of Jamesburg
one OF the injured, told police and
university authorities he and a
classmate invited Miss Katzman
and Miss Corrine R. Pommer, 20, of
Ridgewood, student at the wom-
ems college, to attend a college
dance Saturday night. When they
could not get tickets, they decided
to dance at the fraternity house.


Later, when relatives who might
have put the girls up for the night
could not be located, young Schiff
said it was decided to give them an
unoccupied room on the second floor


Miss Pommer jumped from the
window when the flames cut off her
escape, but Miss Katzman died in
the room. The two sophomores,
Berger and Gordon, died in their
third-foor room before aid could
reach them.


Fire Chief Arthur Jacques said the
fire started from sparks from first
floor fireplace


Earl Reed Silvers, dean of men.
placed Sigma Alpha Mu on indefi-
mite social probation last night for
violation of the university rule for
bidding unchaperoned entertaining
of girls in fraternity houses. He said
the members were suspended from
any fraternity activities.

For many of Natures children,
August is resting month. For
some, time of preparation. Though

pee wee comes at close of day. In

sky the red-shouldered hawk sends

large flocks preparatory to their
southern vacation.

spring brooks dry up. Some streams

chorage may also have the eggs of

places.

oughly bombed and shelled day and

ish Pacific fleet carrier planes and

patriation ship docked. The Amer

quests for special numbers to the
British service band which greeted
them with a blare of music on the
dock. The bandsmen did not know
many Of the newest swing tunes
demanded by the repatriates-and
where the Americans had learned
them, words and all, was a minor
mystery.


The liberated men appeared In
good physical condition, despite the
hardships and dangers they had
but recently survived while escap-
ing from Nazi guards or prison pens
and making their way in the midst
Of battle to the Red Army lines.
They were outfltted in the patch
work remains of Allied uniforms,
including items of Red Army issue.
In the latter category, most notice.
able were the winter fur caps with
upturned flaps.


When the ship docked a pontoon
bridge was rigged from the quay
and across this the British filed
ashore. The Americans remained
aboard.


Some of the United States SOL
diers had been in German hands
for more than two years. Others,
who were caught during the winter
Ardennes offensive, had been held
by the Nazis for only little more
than a month.


Generally, their stories were the
same. They told of a sudden Ger
man panic as the Soviets ap-
preached and a decision to march
the prisoners back into Germany
across Poland's frozen plains. Their
nervous guards themselves were
afraid OF being captured by the
Russians and did not attempt to
hunt for those who managed to
ESCAPE from trains and marching
columns.

and make an appealing pattern
against a winter sky. The ovate
leaves are a glossy shining green
with tiny featherlike veins. When
frost time comes and the seasons
end approaches. the foliage makes
one Of the loveliest sights Of Nature.


Over all the eastern half of the
Nation one finds the sturdy, tall
growing trees They supply wood
for mans uses but they also add
beauty to the landscape. Many a
farmer, working in his woodlot in
the winter, leaves one OF the great
friendly trees as he cuts for the
seasons needs. The countryman
knows that man does not live by
bread alone.

protest, supreme headquarters an
nounced yesterday.

20, was not disclosed. Headquarters

Headquarters gave this account:


The Super Fort was flying over
Russian controlled Korea when
Russian fighter planes intercepted 1t

to land at a nearby airfield.


The big bomber headed toward

to force it to land. Then they made
third pass, shooting out an engine
and the pilot ordered the crew to
bail out.


The report here said all members
of the crew managed to escape.


Gen. MacArthur's protest pointed
out that the Super Fort obviously
was an American plane and had
been shot down after the Japanese
had been ordered to- cease fire and
keep all their planes grounded.


The protest was filed a few days
after the incident. The Russians
replied that the shooting was to be
regretted, that 1t was a mistake, but
that Russian flyers knew some jap
anese planes still were in the air.


The Russians said their pilots
thought the japanese might have
repaired a Super Fort forced down
in Japan and were taking no
chances.


It wasn't learned whether Gen.
Macarthur considered the case
closed.


This was the only known case
where the Russians had any con-
tact with the Americans long range
bomber.

lish on one document.

Health Officer George C. Rutland
today held out hope that the current
outbreak of infantile paralysis has
passed its peak


DR.. Rutland said in the week end
ing Saturday there were only fiva
cases of polio reported in the Dis
trict compared with nine the week
before, which may represent the
peak of this summers outbreak


He explained that last year the
epidemic in the District began with
the report of eight cases during
the third week of July and during
the following eight weeks there were
116 cases reported. This year, how
ever, he said, one case was reported
as early as the first week in June
and during the following eight weeks
of the present outbreak only 25
cases have been reported.


Therefore, for comparable epi-
demic periods of eight weeks, there
we're more than four times the num-
ber OF cases reported last year." DR..
Rutland said


While the departments statement
used the term comparable epidemic
periods, DR.. Rutland concluded his
announcement with the statement
"the department does not feel there
is a re-occurrence of the epidemic
last year


DR.. Rutland said if cases did
occur in a post epidemic year, their
early appearance was to be expected.
He said not only are there fewer
cases for the eight-week period used
in comparing the outbreak with last
year, but there are also fewer para
lytic cases this time Last year dur
ing the eight-week period eight
cases out of every 10 were paralytic
and one person out of five died,
while this year five out of every
10 cases are parlytic and only one
out of every 25th person has died.


This does not necessarily mean
that the disease is milder, but
rather that more nonparalytic cases
have been diagnosed" DR.. Rutland
stated. Furthermore, last year no
suspect polio cases were reported
for the eight-week period, while
this year 81 cases have been ad-
mitted to the hospitals and found
not to be polio. Taking all facts
into consideration, the department
does not feel there is a re-occur-
renee of the epidemic last year"

The current crisis which has arisen
in French Indo- China reveals the
crumbling foundations Of the jerry
built Japanese colonial empire in
Southeastern Asia. For Tokyo it is
doubly serious because, with the
opening of japanese land commune
cations across China. the dominated
French colony is the vital link with
Thailand. Burma, Malaga and the
Dutch Indies, now that the sea lanes
between those countries and Japan
are being ruptured by American air
and naval power exerted from the
Philippines.


French Indo-China was one of the
first prizes in the Japanese campaign
of aggression to the southwark. The
collapse of France to Germany in
the summer of 1910 left it's big Ash
attic colony isolated and exposed to
Axis pressure, since the colonial
authorities gave their allegiance to
the Vichy regime and obeyed its
orders. Accordingly, the governor
general, Admiral Decoux, acceded to
series of japanese demands which
quickly transformed the colony into
virtual japanese protectorate, with
strong japanese forces in the coun-
try. However, the French troops
were not disarmed and the French
administration continued to func-
ton with little direct interference
from Tokyo, This suited Japanese
policy, because it relieved them from
the burden of directly occupying and
governing a region twice as large as
Japan itself with nearly 25.O00.0O0
inhabitants. Also, it threw upon the
French authorities the onus of carry
ing out burdensome economic meas
ures dictated by Tokyo for Japan's
benefit.


The situation began to change
with the liberation of France by the
Allied invasion last summer, the
evaporation of the Vichy regime and
the establishment at Paris of ma
tional government headed by Gen.
eral de Gaulle. When Tokyo put
pressure on Admiral Decoux to dis
avow the new Paris government and
adhere openly to the japanese Co
prosperity sphere" the governor
general first temporized and then
fatty refused. Meanwhile. the Japa-
nese found the French authorities
throughout Indo-China less cooper
alive while the native population
grew FESTIVE and even openly rebel
lious against japanese domination.
All this has prompted the japanese
officials to take drastic measures,
including the disarmament Of the
French troops, white and native,
within the colony. Although full
details are lacking, it seems appar-
ent that the japanese are taking
over full control. This. however,
means that they must assume heavy
burdens in holding down a latently
rebellious Indo-China at the very
moment when Allied pressure is
mounting from without. The indi-
cations are that, for Japan, Indo-
China will soon shift from an asset
into liability.
