In the last two weeks Romania-a
small country compared with the great
European powers-has become the most
sensitive point In the relationship
Z among the Big Three concerning the
carrying out of the Yalta agreements.
Although only meager reports are being
published about developments in Bucha-
rest, the highest authorities in Washing
ton and London admit that they are
concerned.


The Romanian personalities involved
In the recent political seesaw are OF
little consequence. What is Worrying
our State Department and the British
Foreign Once is that so soon after the
Crimea' Conference was ended in full
harmony, the ugly head OF "unlateral
action" seems to have been raised again.


Soon after Mr. Roosevelt,s return to
Washington political crisis developed

who had been appointed Premier of
Romania with the full approval of the
Russian government, was overt thrown
by the new Democratic Front"


Thus far nothing happened to upset
the Yalta apple cart. King Michael adj
vised the representatives of the Big
Three that he was charging Prince
Barbu Stirbey with the task of FORM
ing new government. In the mean
time, Vice Commissar Andri Vishinsky
flew over from Moscow and took the
whole matter in hand. When Stirbey
was unable to form the government,
Peter Groza, man known for COM
munistic leanings, was placed at the
head OF the cabinet. The political views
OF the new Prime Minister are of no
consequence to Washington and Lon
don. But the British and American
governments were astonished that they
had not been consulted when Groza
was selected by Vishinsky to head the
new administration.


During the ministerial crisis. some
OF the highest officials in Romania are
reported to have appealed to American
authorities In Bucharest for shelter on
the plea that their lives were endan-
gered by the purges which the new gov
eminent had pledged itself to carry out.
The Americans informed Washington
that these people had made the appeals
on the ground that they were political
refugees. In order not to upset the
4alta agreement, Washington decided
to turn them down.

During all my service with con-

These fruit bats are unusual, since
their relatives are all insectivorous
animals. But fruit bats have molars
especially designed for crushing
pulpy fruit and never touch animal
matter. They are always in a bad
humor. and though their teeth are
not sharp, they can bruise . finger
they happen to snap.


| Besides having a mean temper,
these creatures are dirty, evil-smell-
ing and noisy They are clad in a
heavy fur coat with a thick mantle
over their shoulders. Some have a
wing expanse of feet or more.
| They do not have tail. This serves
| to identify them from close relatives.


During the day. these night hunt
ers hang en- masse in the top of 8
palm tree. Toward twilight. they
become restless and hungry. One
by one, they drop into the air, flying
in an irregular, wavering line. The,
scream harsh squeaks at each other
as they race toward an orchard or
fruit tree.


Upon locating tree, these hungry
hordes cover its branches. Not sat-
isfied with eating as much as they
can hold, they get into quarrels.
spelling any fruit that may have es-
capped them. The leaves will be
stripped and even the bark torn into
ribbons. When morning comes, they
leave for the top of some tall jungle
tree, where they hang head down
until dusk returns.


In spite of all the superstitions
and legends connected with these
bats, the natives will climb their
tree and club the sleepy ones to
death. They claim that the flesh
when steamed, is tender and de-
licious, with a gamey flavor.

papan area was menaced today
by Australian 7th Division troops,
paced by tanks, spreading out
along the invaded East Borneo
coast under a continuous fire
screen of warships, planes and
artillery.


The tank-led columns were less
than miles from the two-runway
Manggar Airdrome, IL miles to the
northeast of burning Balikpapan,
Borneo's greatest oil port. The Mel
bourne radio said the fall of Balik-
papan is but "a matter of hours"


The armored spearheads operated

sending up scout planes as eyes
for the ground batteries. Busy
engineers expected to have the
cratered 4,600-foot airfield ready for
transport planes soon.


Japs Forced OFF Balance,
Writing from field near Balik-
papan, Associated Press Core
spondent Russell Brines gave this
overall summary today:


Enemy forces in this area appar-
emily were toppled off balance and
ripped into small units, lacking COM
munications, by the intense pre-
landing bombardmentS. They have
failed to regain their equilibrium in
the face of the swift Aussie advance
Hence, they we're unable to take ad-
vantage of the intensive fortifica-
tions they prepared long ago."


He reported that the Aussies, after
uncovering 500 enemy mines, still
were plagued by the most ingenious
maze of concealed demolitions and
BOBBY traps yet encountered in the
Southwest Pacific. Mr.. Brines said
the Japanese probably will put up a
strong defense along the highway
leading north from Balikpapan SO
miles to Marinda in the heart of the
main oil fields.


From the last ridges before Balik-
papan, Associated Press Correspand-
ent James Hutcheson looked down
on wrecked reflneries, smashed by
Allied air and naval attacks.
Restoration Job Begun.


Now engineers stand ready to be-
gin the tremendous job of restoring
them, but Mt. Hutcheson said it was
likely that the oil fields serving them
would remain in enemy hands for
some time. The Aussies near Balik-
papan had made the deepest inland
penetration from Sundays invasion
beaches-2 miles.


The capture of Sepinggang air.
field against light opposition gave
Gen. MacArthur's forces a base
within fighter plane range of Java
and afforded the United States 7th
Fleet air cover on runs deep inside
Makassar Straits, until recently
penetrated only by Allied subma-
rineS.

ment in Washington of the recent
sinking of the Japanese heavy cruis-
er Ashiguru by the British subma-

Java and Singapore indicated that
already a tight net has been drawn

Tomatoes lettuce and radishes - they can't

New OPA regulations designed to
control rental rates for taxis will
not affect CPA suits now pending
against 154 taxicab feet operators
in the District. In these suits dam

to individual drivers.

the District Office of Price Admins
tration, made this announcement

inquiries that developed after the

complete new set Of taxicab regu-

require fleet operators and others
who rent taxicabs to individual driv-
ers to file their current rates, to-
gether with rent rate schedules of
March, 1912, with the Transporta-
ton and Public Utilities Division of
the national OPA.


The OPA filed its suits for treble
damages against the 154 operators
last August and in December Justice
Matthew Mcclure Of District Court
ruled that OPA had Jurisdiction over
rental rates here. The operators
have appeals pending.

A freak fire and explosion late
yesterday blew the front out of the
Lady Arlington Beauty Salon, 926
South Willmore street, when a gas
water heater ignited nail polish re-
mover that fell from a broken half
gallon bottle, Fire Chief A. C. Schel-
fel reported today.


The fire started, he said, when one
of the operators picked up the bottle
and the bottom fell out, spilling the
liquid, which ignited and spread to
other bottles nearby. All occupants
of the shop rushed outside.


The explosion followed when the
operator forced open the door in
an effort to retrieve her coat. Gas
pressure had held it closed and when
it was opened admission of oxygen
caused the explosion. Several school
children received scratches from
flying glass as they were passing the
salon. Arlington and Jefferson fire
companies extinguished the blaze.
Firemen estimated damage at "sev-
eral hundred" dollars.

WASHINGTON. July y tUP)
The navy has under considera-
tion today a discharge system for
older officers and enlisted men
based only on age and length of
service.


In announcing the tentative
plan the navy estimated a total
of 10000 officers and men would
be eligible for discharge under the
system by next December.


MINIMUM POINTS


The minimum points needed
range from 50 TO 81 depending on
the branch in which the men are
serving.


Under the plan a mans service
age" is computed by allowing one
point for each year of his age TO
his nearest birthday plus addi-
tional points for each four months
of active duty since Sept. l. 1899.


Reserve officers of the line, en-
listed reServistS, inductees and
enlisted regulars serving despite
expired enlistments would need
SO points for discharge.


RESERVE OFFICERS


Reserve officers of supply would
need 55 points while civil engineer
reserve officers would need 81.
The navy explained the higher
score were necessary because
those two branches have fewer
officers.


Regular navy officers are not
included in the program except
when they are temporary officers
with a regular enlisted status.

The Cape Fear River, out of it's
banks in one of the States worst
floods in years, left thousands home
less today and caused untold damage
to crops and buildings in this south
eastern section of North Carolina.


Red Cross officials said last night
that $500 persons already had been
evacuated from flooded areas and
that the total was expected to
reach at least $500 today.


Fayetteville was about 20 to 25

workers estimated. Widespread low
lying areas were heavily awash.


Army Aids Homeless.


The town of Dunn, about 25 miles

and other public buildings into sane
tuaries for evacuees.

Bragg aided in moving marooned
and homeless victims to safety.
Servicemen constructed a tent city
in which hundreds were given
shelter.


With the water receding in some
sections, the worst was expected to-
be over today. Richard N Hart, in
charge of Red Cross activities, said.


Highway System ParaIyzed. !


The 17lst Evacuation Hospital
was placed in full operation here
and the Army also joined in provid-
ing food for the victims. Military
police. State highway patrolmen
and Red Cross workers united in
directing traffic and other problems.


School buildings and other struc-
lures here also were placed at the
disposal of the homeless and des-
titute.


The State Highway Department
reported the highway system in the
eastern part of the State paralyzed.
Some roads, however, were opened
as the foodwaters receded.


United States Highway l, blocked
Wednesday night south of Rocking
ham, was reported open today. Also
reported as opened, was North Caro-
lima highway 81 from Fayetteville
to Sanford. Fayetteville hitherto
had been marooned, since all major
highways leading into it were in
undated.

Soviet scientists have discovered

pines broke 400-year old custom
today when horse-drawn calesas,
caribao carts and motorized traffic
started travelling on the right side
Of streets and highways instead of
the left.


The changeover, to conform with
the United States traffic practice,
was ordered by the American Army,
whose vehicles are built for right
side driving.


Impetus for the change also came
from Manila automobile dealers
who handle American-built cars.


Signs advising the public of the
changeover have been posted for
weeks but military police anticipate
some trouble. They pointed out
that many American Army jeep and
truck drivers have become used to
left-side travel in Australia, New
Guinea and the Philippines during
the last two or three years.

Inquiries would indicate great in
terest on the part of many readers
concerning the oyster catchers.
There are three species in North
America: all are essentially mari
time birds.


They are found only along ocean
fronts, where they get most of
their food. They are expert catch
ers OF oysters, mussels. CLAIMS ana
various Shellflsh, and also are fond
OF marine worms and insects.


Oyster catcherS have sturdy legs
and strong feet from which the
hind toe is missing. The plumage
is mostly black on the upper parts
and almost pure white underneath.
Their bill is a brilliant red. When
walking along the shore, they as
sumo a most deliberate and dignifled
stride. They can break into a run
with considerable speed. Their fight
is in keeping with their swift get
away. and it is graceful. When
flushed, the catcher merely rises
from harms way.


No nest is built for the Young,
The three eggs are usually laid in a
depression in the sand. AS they are
bun white, blotched and freckled
with dark brown, they are not read
lily seen. The mother cares for her
eggs at night and in cloudy weather,
letting the sun and hot sands take
care of them at other times.


The American oyster catcher in
habits the coasts of our Southeastern
States. The other two forms, in
cluding species that is almost
dark all over, live on the Pacific
Coast. All have such strong, OYSTER
knife bills and strongly shod feet
that they are able to walk over the
sharp-edged oyster beds without
harm. Oysters and CLAIMS, waiting
for their food, lie just below the
sand with shells wide open. The
birds are not at all disturbed when
the heavy shells close fast. The
oyster catcher can wait until the
bivalve gives up. or it can lift its
foot and open the vise-like clasp
with its own special oyster knife.

An 9Th Air Force staff officer said
targets included important military
and governmental Office buildings,

THE attack was aimed at disrupt

yesterday after Thursdays nation

porters.

Certain birds with dark feathers
sometimes gather around COWS in
a pasture Known as "cowbirds," !"
they dart around after insects which
hover about the COWS.


Cowbirds found in Canada and
the United States are almost as
large as robins. The males have
greenish- black feathers on the body,
but are brown about the head. The
females are gray-brown.


Several other names are used for
cowbirds. Some persons call them
cow blackbirds," others Cow bunt-
ings' or lazy birds"


The name lazy bird" takes us
to a strange habit of these feathered
creatures. The females are too lazy
to build their own nests. They do
not even warm their own eggs, but
leave the work to other birds!


Going about in a flock which
contains both males and females, a
female cowbird will slip away from
the rest and lay an egg in some
ready-made nest nearby. Then she
returns to the flock.


Dozens OF kinds of birds build
nests which are used for cowbird
eggs. Ginning sparrows, yellow

DAMASCUS, May 80 DelayeO -
This Syrian capital was in chaos
today after an all-night French
bombardment, and late reports from
Hama said the situation there was
equally bad. with British military
authorities receiving what they de-
scribed as "piteous appeals" for
relief.


Indiscriminate firing thus far
probably has cost 300 lives and
threatens to cost many more.
The latest report from Hama put
the casualties in today's fighting
there at more than 200. The town
was reported being bombed and
under fire from arms of all sorts.


There appears to be no solution IN
sight except outright British Amer
ican seizure of control. A high
French officer said the French must
be firm" and the Syrians are de-
termined not to bow, feeling that
giving in would prejudice their in
dependence.


British and American authorities
In Syria and Lebanon were reported
to have told Gen. Humboldt, French
commander in the two countries,
that the bloodshed was absolutely
indefensible."


The violence erupted at 6:55 pm.
Tuesday. Artillery, mortar and ma
chine-gun fire, as well as aerial
bombs, rained on Damascus almost
increasingly. Syrian gendarmes
answered the fire with every avail
able weapon.


Damascus exploded into chaos
after week of high tension over
French insistence on Syrian and
Lebanese acceptance of a treaty
giving France special rights. They
accompanied their demands by
landing new troops in the Levant
states.


Crowds gathered daily before the
serail government house, and
other government installations. de-
manding action against the French
The sight of French troops would
provoke instant trouble. usually in
the form of shooting.


Tuesday night four Syrian SOL
diers from Troopes Speciales Levees
conscripts under French command
attempted to desert into the crowd
between the serail and the French
barracks. The French fired at them
Somebody in the crowd fired back


Almost precisely the same thing
had occurred repeatedly in the last
few days. Syrian government gen.
darmes took charge Immediately
dispersed the crowds and put quick
end to the disorders or managed
to localize the fighting.
But this time. although the gen.
darmerie went into action quickly
the entire area around the serail
burst into a din of fire from all
sides.


French State Policy.
The French said they were fired
on first by the Syrians. The Syrians
claim the French were ready and
waiting in positions surrounding the
serail. ready to open fire at signal
The French have informed both
American and British authorities Of
f1cially that their policy was tc
"intimidate" the Syrian populace
and that they saw no other way OF
handling the situation.
The Syrians decline to be intimi-
dated and thus far have given every
evidence of standing firm to the
bitter end.

MANILA, July 8 Sunday -
Australian 7th Division troops
have pushed 6 miles northeast
ward beyond the now-secured
Borneo oil port of Balikpapan
and are thrusting steadily inland
from Penadjam Point, across
Balikpapan Bay, a Southwest
Pacific communique reported
today.


Other elements of the same Aus
tralian division were driving
northward toward the Sambodja
and Samarinda oil fields, % and 55
miles, respectively, northeast of
Balikpapan. Mined roads and ar
tillery fire were used by the with
drawing enemy to defend these last
two important Japanese-held oil
areas.


One japanese plane raided the
Balikpapan area without result, and
Allied planes, supporting the ground
offensive, ranged at will over Bor-
neo," Gen. MacArthur's communi-
que said. Two Japanese freighters
we're destroyed at the southern port
of Bandjermasin.


Japs in Difficult Spot.


In their flight northward, the
Japanese had the choice of a death
stand, surrender in the marshy oil
lands, or escape into the unexplored
jungle domain of the head-hunting
Dyaks to the westward.


The Dyaks probably will finish
them off," said Capt. J. w. zylstra
of Amsterdam, commander of a
Netherlands unit of Indonesians and
West Indians scouting for the Aus
sizes. Poisonous snakes and insects
are other hazards of the jungle.


Balikpapan was secured Thursday
with a swift cross-bay thrust in
which the Australians captured
Penadjam Point, putting Japanese
coastal batteries out of action.


But the Aussies met stiff opposi-
tion in hand-to-hand fighting with
an enemy naval ground force de-
Tending the PandanSari refinery
north of Balikpapan.


First Phase of Campaign Ends.


Capture of Penadjam Point,
achieved with the aid of American
manned amphibious craft, put a
swift end to the first f1ve-day phase
Of the campaign, which is ahead of
schedule, Associated Press Cerre-
spondent Russell Brines reported
from the battle zone.


The speedy five-day initial opera
ton gave the Aussies command of
10 miles Of the coast, from Pendjam
to Manggar airfield to the north
east, and two airflelds-the 1000
foot strip at Manggar and Seping-
gan drome.


Mr.. Brines said the Japanese
around Balikpapan had some of
the strongest defenses Allied forces
had encountered In the Southwest
Pacific, but the enemy chose to
withdraw its main force from the
invasion poundings of Allied war
ships and planes.


1880 Tons of Shells Fired.


Rear Admiral Albert G. Noble
said the Allied warships had fired
more than 1,250 tons of shells, while
bombers had hit the Japanese shore
positions with 5000 tons of ex-
plosiveS.


Australian casualties, which would
have been heavy had the Japs stayed
to fight on the shore, were remark
ably low. Headquarters reported
yesterday that 214 Aussies had been
killed, with % more missing and
420 wounded.


Japanese dead, counted through
all Borneo operations including the
Australian invaSions on the north
coast, were 3,03l, headquarters said.
Prisoners totaled 274.

By the Associated Press.


TOKYO, Dec. l0.-Continuine
his roundup of war criminal sus-
poets, Gen. Macarthur today
directed the arrest of 81 Japa-
nese accused of committing
atrocities against United Nations
nationals held in the Cabana-
tuan prison camp in the Phil
ippines, in prisons, camps and
hospitals in Japan proper and
on the prisoner-of-war ship
Oryoku Maru during the vessels
nightmarish voyage from the
Philippines to Japan.


Also ordered arrested were three
Japanese naval officers. including a
repatriate from Wake Island. Two
of them are being court -martialed
by the japanese.


New Suspects Small Fry"


The newest war criminal suspects
were considered small fry" in COM
parison with some of the japanese
arrested recently, but to American
and Allied prisoners of war they
ranked highest.


Included was 1t. Col. BANJO Mori
who commanded the Cabanatuan
prison camp from 1912 to 1914, and
Col. Gennosuke Mona, who directed
japanese gendarmerie in Hong Kong
from December, 1912, to February,
1o45.


Also named were a 1t Toshino
and a civilian interpreter known
only as Wada Both were aboard
the Oryoku Maru between Deem
ber, 1914, and January, l945, when
they were accused of atrocities.


Three Others Surrender.


Three japanese named on pre-
vious war criminal suspect lists sur
rendered today at Sugamo Prison.
They were Gen. Jinzaburo Mazaki,
once inspector general of military
education; Nagakage Okabe, who
was education minister in the cabi-
net of ex-Premier Hideki TOTO, and
Koichiro Ishigara. businessman.


American fears of an assasSina-
ton attempt against Mazaki-a pos
sible key witness against Tojo-
ended today when he surrendered.


Mazaki. who also faces war
crimes trial. has indicated through
a brother that among other teSti-
mony at his trial he will charge
TOTO and his cohorts plunged
Japan into the Pacific conflict pri-
marily to avoid the peoples wrath
for failure in the China war.


With Mazaki's incarceration, 1t
can be revealed reliably that Amer
ican authorities feared japanese
extremists might try to silence the
69-year-old general 1t was con-
sidered likely that impetus for such
a plot might come from recently
demobilized colonies and majors
who originally supported TOTO and
who actually ran the japanese War
Ministry after Tojo's cabinet fell.


Rice Riots Threatened.


Meanwhile, a warning from in
f1uential farmers that rice riots are
inevitable without stronger govern
ment agrarian policies conceded to-
day with Gen. MacArthur's second
blunt demand that Japan's feudal
land system be altered Immediately.


Fifteen farmer representatives
from Akita Province in Northeastern
Japan declared muddled govern
ment policies have produced such
lack of confidence that the rich To-
hoku district may sell only so per
cent of its rice crop to the govern
ment.


Gen. MacArthur's land directive
abolishes absentee land ownership
and provides that millions of farm
ers may buy land on long term at
low rates.


Crises Feared.


The measure threatens new
crisis for Premier Kijuro Shide-
hara's cabinet, which is on the verge
of collapse. Gen. MacArthurs' first
demand last month for agrarian re-
form resulted in lukewarm gov
ernment measure now before hesi-
tant diet. Today's directive cracks
the whip for prompt action on a
reform which the landowners are
opposing strongly.


The farmers warning of rice riots
followed their meeting with Prince
Higashi- former premier, in
which they asked that the Emperor
be invited to visit Tohoku prefecture
to "dispel the mental confusion now
existing among agricultural commu-
mites" They said only an imperial
visit would enable farmers to regain
their confidence and stability"


Their compatriots, the farmers
added, have lost confidence in the
Central Government and perfectural
authorities, and are refusing to sell
their rice. Without a full quota

STANLEY, N. Dak., Sept. L.
Mrs. Lena Molzhon, 70, credits
her dog with saving her life
twice when she was attacked by
a COW with a newborn calf
Tuesday afternoon.

drove the enraged cow away
after it had knocked her down,
breaking her hip and dislocat-
ing her shoulder.


Then, said Mrs. Molzhon, the
dog lay down close beside her
and kept her warm throughout
the night. Mrs. Molzhon was
found lying in the pasture, the
dog still close beside her, 28
hours later by a son-in-law.


In a Mino hospital, where she
was reported in good condition,
Mrs. Molzhon said she believes
she could not have survived the
chilly night If 1t had not been
for the dog.

LONDON, Jan. 18. Flying
Fortresses today bombed Kaisers-
lautern, an important German
rail yard behind the Saar front.


Raj bombers returned to the Ger
man industrial center of Magdeburg
with q new load Of explosives just
before dawn and found parts of the
city still ablaze from Tuesday nights
attack.


Striking about 5 am, the raiders
caught the Germans by surprise,
dropped their bomb loads and re-
turned home without loss, the Air
Ministry said.


The early morning raid signalized
the sixth straight day of an all-out
assault upon German fuel resources
and vital war industries hundreds
of miles behind the front lines.


The dawn raiders were identified
by the Air Ministry as Mosquitoes
carrying two-ton blockbusters.


Ten bombers and five fighters
were lost yesterday by the 9Th Air
Force in sweeping attacks upon u
boat pens and oil plants around
Hamburg and railyards at Pader-
born. Seven hundred bombers and
$50 fighters participated.


Bad weather limited aerial opera
tions over the battle front yesterday.

TORONTO, Nov. Halloween

youthful mob which officers estimat-
ed at 1000 stormed a police station
in vain attempt to free Is persons
arrested for an earlier disturbance.


Mounted and foot police and hose
welding firemen repulsed the rush.
Five firenen and two police officers
were injured. Two youths required
hospital attention for head cuts.


Observers said the action developed
after a number of teen-agers set
fires on Queen street, feeding them
with wood from fences and res
licences, dumped cement blocks into
the roadway and emptied gasoline
down streetcar rails and ignited it.


Police were jeered and stoned
when they made arrests.
